title: GOD STRUCK ONAN DEAD… BUT WAS IT REALLY BECAUSE OF WHAT HE DID IN BED?
paragraphs: GOD STRUCK ONAN DEAD… BUT WAS IT REALLY BECAUSE OF WHAT HE DID IN BED?
The disturbing truth behind Genesis 38:8–10 reveals a betrayed widow, a man who wanted the pleasure without the responsibility, and a God who saw the injustice everyone else was willing to ignore.
What if the sin that brought judgment upon Onan was far deeper than the physical act most people have been taught to condemn?
A woman had already buried her husband.
She had already endured the kind of grief that changes the sound of a home. The empty place beside her. The future she thought she would have. The children she might never hold.
And now, the man who was supposed to help preserve her deceased husband's family line was using the very arrangement meant to protect her for his own advantage.
He came close enough to take what he wanted.
But he deliberately withheld what he had been called upon to give.
And Scripture says God saw it.
Then, in one of the most unsettling moments in Genesis, the Lord put him to death.
For centuries, people have argued about the physical act. But the biblical narrative asks us to confront something much bigger.
What happens when a person uses another human being while deliberately refusing the responsibility that comes with that relationship?
What happens when someone appears to fulfill an obligation while secretly sabotaging its purpose?
And what happens when the person being wronged has almost no power to defend herself?

To understand why God judged Onan, we must enter the world of Genesis 38, not through the assumptions of our own century, but through the family obligations, inheritance customs, moral failures, and redemptive storyline of Scripture.
Because buried inside this uncomfortable account is something astonishing.
The story that exposes Onan's wickedness also belongs to the family history through which Jesus Christ would eventually come into the world.
And that changes how we read everything.
Before Onan, there was Er.
Before the scandal, there was a marriage.
And before Tamar became a woman caught in a desperate family crisis, she was someone's wife.
Genesis 38 tells us that Judah, one of Jacob's sons, had three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah.
Judah arranged for his firstborn, Er, to marry a woman named Tamar.
But the marriage did not become the beginning of the family Tamar had hoped for.
Genesis 38:7 tells us that Er was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord put him to death.
The Bible does not tell us the particular wickedness Er committed. That silence matters. We must not invent accusations where God has not provided details.
What we do know is that Tamar was left widowed and, as the narrative subsequently makes clear, without a child to carry forward her deceased husband's family line.
In the ancient Israelite family world, that was not merely a private disappointment.
A widow's security, place within the household, and future could be deeply connected to family relationships, offspring, and inheritance.
This is where Onan entered the story.
Judah commanded his second son to fulfill a family obligation toward Tamar.
Genesis 38:8 records:
"Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother." (KJV)
Those words can sound strange to modern ears.
Why would a man be told to marry his deceased brother's widow?
Was this about sexual access?
Was this about forcing a marriage?
Or was there a larger family responsibility involved?
The answer lies in an ancient practice later regulated in Israel's law, commonly called levirate marriage.
The term comes from the Latin levir, meaning a husband's brother.

Deuteronomy 25:5–10 later describes an arrangement in which a surviving brother was expected to marry his childless deceased brother's widow so that the dead brother's name would not disappear from Israel.
Importantly, Genesis 38 takes place before that Mosaic legislation was given. We should not pretend that every provision of Deuteronomy 25 was already legally operating in exactly the same form.
Nevertheless, the underlying family custom is unmistakably present.
The purpose was not simply to produce a child.
It was to preserve the deceased brother's name and family continuity, with significant implications for the widow and the household.
And Onan knew what was expected.
The Hebrew text makes that painfully clear.
Genesis 38:9 begins:
וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Vayyēdaʿ ʾÔnān kî lōʾ lô yihyeh hazzāraʿ.
A close rendering is:
"And Onan knew that the offspring would not be his."
That one sentence reveals something important about his motive.
Onan was not acting in ignorance.
He understood the family arrangement.
He knew that the child born through this obligation would be reckoned as continuing his deceased brother's line rather than simply advancing his own.
And he did not want that.

Perhaps inheritance interests played a role. Perhaps resentment or selfish ambition contributed. The text does not explicitly disclose every calculation in his mind, so we should not claim certainty about motives Scripture leaves unstated.
But it does reveal the decisive fact.
He knew the obligation.
And he intentionally frustrated it.
Genesis 38:9 continues in the King James Version:
"And it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother."
The Hebrew uses the expression:
וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה
Veshiḥēt ʾarṣāh.
In this context, it describes his deliberately wasting semen on the ground rather than allowing conception.
The physical action is part of the account. We should neither erase it nor turn away from what Scripture actually says.
But notice the explanatory words attached to it.
"Lest that he should give seed to his brother."
There is the stated purpose behind his behavior.
He was deliberately preventing the outcome that the family obligation was intended to secure.
The text is not describing a man who accidentally failed to conceive a child.
It is not describing an infertile couple.
And it is not merely presenting a detached discussion of reproductive biology.
It describes a man repeatedly entering a sexual relationship with his brother's widow while intentionally preventing the very offspring he was expected to help provide.
The Hebrew construction in Genesis 38:9 presents his conduct as characteristic or repeated when he had relations with Tamar, rather than clearly identifying one isolated occurrence.
Imagine what that meant for her.
She had already lost her husband.
Now the surviving brother was participating in the arrangement while secretly defeating its central purpose.
She remained without the heir the arrangement was supposed to make possible.
Her future remained uncertain.
And the man who understood the obligation was acting against it.
We are not told Tamar's private thoughts during those encounters. Scripture does not record her words or explicitly describe her emotional experience at this point.
But we can recognize the vulnerability of her situation without pretending to know everything she felt.
She was a widow in a patriarchal household, dependent upon decisions being made by men who controlled the arrangements affecting her future.
And the man expected to help was not acting faithfully.
Then comes the verse that has troubled readers for generations.
Genesis 38:10:
"And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also." (KJV)
In Hebrew, the verse begins:
וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
Vayyēraʿ beʿênê YHWH ʾăsher ʿāsāh.
A close translation is:
"And what he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD."
Notice the language.
The narrator does not simply say that Onan broke a family custom.
He says that what Onan did was evil before God.
But here we must be careful.
Some interpretations have treated this passage as though it were primarily a universal prohibition of every act of non-procreative sexual intercourse or every form of contraception.
Other interpretations have dismissed the physical behavior as completely irrelevant and claimed that the passage concerns only a technical inheritance violation.
Neither simplification does full justice to the narrative.
The text explicitly describes Onan's physical action and explicitly connects it to his intention not to provide offspring for his brother.
His wrongdoing must be understood in that narrative context.

The passage does not, by itself, settle every broader Christian ethical question about contraception, marital intimacy, or reproductive choices. Those questions require consideration of the wider biblical witness and, among Christians, have received different theological interpretations.
What Genesis 38 makes unmistakable is that Onan knowingly and deliberately undermined a serious family responsibility while continuing to participate in the sexual arrangement.
He wanted the relationship on terms that benefited him while defeating the responsibility attached to it.
And God judged his conduct as evil.
There is another important distinction.
The later law in Deuteronomy 25 describes a public procedure for a brother who refuses the levirate obligation. It does not prescribe death as the ordinary legal penalty for refusal.
That means we should not carelessly conclude that God struck Onan dead simply because every refusal to enter such a marriage automatically deserved execution.
Onan's conduct involved more than openly declining the arrangement.
He entered it and deliberately sabotaged its purpose.
The narrative presents God's judgment as a direct divine act, not as a penalty Israel was subsequently instructed to administer to every similar offender.
That distinction protects us from turning a specific biblical judgment into a rule Scripture itself does not establish.
But it also prevents us from softening the moral seriousness of the story.
Because Onan's sin was not hidden from God.
And neither was Tamar.
There is a moment in this account that should make every reader uncomfortable.
Onan could have appeared obedient from the outside.
He was doing what Judah told him to do, at least in outward form.
He was entering the relationship.
He was fulfilling the visible part.
But in the place where no one else could easily inspect his intentions, he was deliberately preventing the obligation from reaching its intended result.
That is the terrifying contrast.
Outward participation. Inward rebellion.
And suddenly this ancient story reaches beyond the ancient world.
Because it is possible to appear faithful while quietly refusing the very obedience God is calling us to practice.
It is possible to speak about love while withholding commitment.
To speak about family while neglecting those who depend on us.
To speak about righteousness while exploiting another person's vulnerability.
To appear generous while calculating only what we will receive.
To participate in religious activity while protecting a secret pattern of selfishness.
Not every failure is the same as Onan's sin. Not every broken relationship involves the same obligations, motives, or circumstances.
But the moral question reaches us.
Are we merely performing the appearance of faithfulness, or are we actually loving our neighbors before God?
Jesus confronted that difference throughout His earthly ministry.
In Matthew 23:27–28, He rebuked religious hypocrisy: outward righteousness masking inward corruption.
In Matthew 15:8, He quoted the prophet Isaiah concerning people whose lips honored God while their hearts remained far from Him.
And in Mark 12:40, He condemned religious leaders who exploited vulnerable widows while maintaining an impressive appearance of devotion.
The God revealed in Jesus Christ is not impressed by religious appearances that conceal injustice.
He sees the person the powerful overlook.
He hears the cry that never reaches a courtroom.
He knows the truth behind a respectable reputation.
And that should both sober and comfort us.
Sober us, because hidden selfishness is not hidden from Him.
Comfort us, because neither is hidden suffering.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be Tamar in some small but painful way.
Not because your circumstances are identical to hers.
But because someone made a promise, and you were the one left carrying the consequences when they failed to keep it.
Someone took your trust but withheld honesty.
Someone benefited from your loyalty but refused to honor their responsibility.
Someone spoke of love while making decisions that left you vulnerable.
And perhaps the hardest part was that everyone else thought they were doing the right thing.
You saw another side.
God saw it too.
Yet the story becomes even more disturbing.
After Onan's death, Judah told Tamar to remain a widow in her father's house until his youngest son, Shelah, grew older.
But Genesis 38:11 reveals that Judah feared Shelah might also die like his brothers.
Later, the narrative makes clear that Judah had not given Shelah to Tamar when he had grown up.
Tamar was left waiting for a promised future that was not being provided.
Then the account takes a shocking turn.
Tamar disguised herself, and Judah, not recognizing her, had sexual relations with her. She conceived.
When Judah later heard that Tamar was pregnant, he called for severe punishment.
The man who had failed in his responsibility toward her was now ready to condemn her.
But Tamar produced the personal items Judah had given her as a pledge.
And suddenly the truth came into the open.
Genesis 38:26 records Judah's astonishing confession:
"She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son." (KJV)
Read that again.
"She hath been more righteous than I."
Judah finally acknowledged his own failure.
This does not mean Scripture is presenting every action in the chapter as a timeless model for believers to imitate.
The narrative is morally complex, and it should remain morally complex.
But Judah's confession identifies a crucial injustice: he had withheld the fulfillment of the obligation he had promised.
The family patriarch who was prepared to judge Tamar had to confront his own wrongdoing.
And there is a warning here for anyone who finds it easier to expose another person's disgrace than to confess their own sin.
Sometimes the scandal we are quickest to condemn is the one that reveals what we have been hiding.
But do not stop reading Genesis 38.
Because the story does not end with death, deception, and disgrace.
Tamar gave birth to twins.
Their names were Perez and Zerah.
And Perez's name would appear again in a place that many readers never expect.
Matthew 1.
The genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:3 says:
"And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar..." (KJV)
In modern English spelling, that is Judah, Perez, Zerah, and Tamar.
Yes.
Tamar is named in the family history of Jesus Christ.
The woman whose story had been surrounded by bereavement, betrayal, uncertainty, and scandal was not erased from the record of the Messiah's ancestry.
Through Perez, the genealogical line recorded in Matthew continues toward David and ultimately Jesus.
This is not proof that God approved of every human action that occurred in Genesis 38.
He did not.
The text has already shown us His judgment against wickedness.
Rather, it reveals something breathtaking about divine providence.
Human sin did not prevent God from carrying forward His redemptive purpose.
And the shame attached to a family's history did not cause God to abandon His promise.
That is where the Gospel begins to shine through this dark account.
Not because Onan secretly represents every sinner in a perfect one-to-one comparison.
Not because Tamar's story should be reduced to a convenient symbol.
But because the larger biblical story reveals a God who judges evil, exposes injustice, preserves His promises, and brings redemption through a family line filled with deeply imperfect human beings.
And that family line leads us to Jesus.
The Son of God did not come into a spotless human family history.
He entered a world already scarred by sin.
He came among people who betrayed, deceived, exploited, abandoned, and failed one another.
He came for sinners.
But He did not come to excuse sin.
He came to save sinners from it.
Matthew 1:21 declares:
"And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." (KJV)
That is the difference between cheap reassurance and biblical grace.
Grace does not tell the unrepentant heart that selfishness is harmless.
Grace calls sinners out of darkness.
Grace confronts what we have tried to justify.
Grace offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again.
Grace begins the work of transforming people who could never make themselves righteous through appearances.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
And Romans 5:8 tells us that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Not after we had successfully cleaned up our family histories.
Not after we had erased every humiliating chapter.
Not after we had become impressive enough to deserve mercy.
Christ came because we needed saving.
And perhaps that is the deepest reason Genesis 38 still matters.
The chapter refuses to flatter humanity.
It shows us the destructive reality of selfishness.
It exposes failures of responsibility.
It reveals the vulnerability of someone whose future depended upon others acting faithfully.
It shows us the seriousness of divine judgment.
And then, within the wider story of Scripture, it reminds us that God's saving purpose is greater than the wreckage human beings create.
If you have been wronged, do not confuse God's patience with indifference.
The Lord sees injustice, even when earthly accountability is delayed or incomplete.
If you have been the one who acted selfishly, do not confuse God's mercy with permission to continue.

Repentance means turning toward God, confessing the truth, and seeking to walk in obedience. Where we have wronged others, genuine repentance should also move us toward appropriate accountability and repair, wherever that is possible and safe.
And if your past contains chapters you are ashamed to remember, do not assume that shame has the final word.
Jesus Christ is not powerless before a ruined reputation.
He is the Savior who died and rose again.
He does not promise that every earthly consequence will disappear.
He promises forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
That is better than pretending the past never happened.
That is redemption.
And before you leave this story, I want to ask you something personal.
Not whether you have memorized the Hebrew words.
Not whether you can win a theological argument about Onan.
But whether there is an area of your life where you have been giving God the appearance of obedience while withholding your heart.
A responsibility you keep avoiding.
A truth you refuse to confess.
A person you have treated unfairly.
A pattern you know needs to change.
Or perhaps you are the one who has spent years carrying the consequences of somebody else's unfaithfulness.
You need to hear this.
Your suffering does not make you invisible to God.
And someone else's sin does not have the authority to define your worth.
Look to Christ.
The One who sees what is hidden is also the One who calls the weary to Himself.
The One who judges wickedness is also the One who offers mercy to repentant sinners.
The One whose genealogy includes Tamar is the One who entered our broken world to accomplish a redemption no human being could achieve.
So do not walk away from Genesis 38 merely asking why Onan died.
Ask what his story reveals about the God before whom we live.
A God who sees.
A God who judges justly.
A God who cares about faithfulness.
A God who does not abandon His promises.
And a God who has revealed His saving grace in Jesus Christ.
Your testimony may encourage someone who thought they were the only one struggling.
We want this to be a place where biblical truth is not diluted, difficult questions are not avoided, and Jesus Christ remains at the center of everything.
That mission also needs people willing to stand behind it.
You do not have to pay to receive God's grace, to prove your faithfulness, or to belong to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
Christ is not for sale.
The Gospel is the good news of what Jesus Christ has accomplished for sinners through His death and resurrection.
Our desire is simply to keep pointing people toward Him.
Onan's story reminds us that God sees what human beings try to conceal.
Tamar's story reminds us that those whom others overlook are not forgotten in God's redemptive purposes.
Judah's confession reminds us that repentance begins when we stop defending ourselves and acknowledge the truth.
And the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that the failures of a family do not have the final word over the promises of God.
The chapter that began with a widow denied a future became part of the family history of the Savior who offers sinners an eternal hope.
